evidence_quotes.quote: In this research, we make a comparative analysis of three regulatory regimes on the extent to which they are consumer-inclusive in the water pricing process.

In this paper, we have explored the existence of mechanisms that foster transparency, participation, and accountability in price regulation of water services in The Netherlands, Barcelona, and Scotland. Each of the cases represents a different regulatory regime, namely self-regulation, bipartite negotiation, and independent regulation, respectively.

To select relevant cases for the study at hand, a key criterion was the existence of a water pricing process under different regulatory regimes (see Table 1). In this respect, we selected the case of Vitens from The Netherlands to represent a self-regulatory regime, the case of Agbar, in Barcelona, to represent bipartite negotiation, and the case of Scottish Water, in Scotland, to represent an independent regulatory regime.

The selection of this subset is motivated by the observation by Hern et al. (2005) that consumer inclusion subsumes three regulatory governance principles, i.e., informing consumers (transparency), resolving consumers’ complaints (accountability) and requesting consumer input (participation).

Care was taken to have similar characteristics in the three cases, apart from the regulatory regime. All three cases are relatively large companies situated in Western Europe with similar levels of water services provision.

criterion_notes.c1: Does not examine household or community water or sanitation service access; instead investigates procedural consumer inclusiveness (transparency, stakeholder participation, and institutional accountability) in utility tariff-setting processes across three Western European cases selected for having similarly high existing coverage.
criterion_notes.c2: Passes the plain wording of Criterion 2 (YES under plain wording) because it examines economic regulatory regimes (self-regulation, bipartite contract negotiation, and independent regulation) and statutory/administrative rules governing information disclosure, public consultation, and appeals in water pricing. Fails the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading (NO under narrow reading) because the legal and regulatory mechanisms examined govern procedural stakeholder voice in regulatory price reviews rather than directly governing household or community service access, eligibility, disconnection, or tariff affordability. Even under the plain wording of Criterion 2, the study remains excluded because it fails Criteria 1 and 4.
criterion_notes.c3: Empirical qualitative comparative case study of three water pricing regulatory regimes based on key informant interviews (regulators, service providers, public authorities, and consumer representative bodies) and secondary/legal document analysis.
criterion_notes.c4: No outcome relevant to service access, connection, availability, reliability, continuity, quantity, affordability, or exclusion is evaluated. The empirical outcomes reported (Table 3) are comparative institutional governance ratings (Lowest/Middle/Highest) of procedural transparency, stakeholder participation, and accountability in tariff setting; 2007 coverage and average annual water cost figures in Table 2 are descriptive case-selection context showing comparability across cases rather than analyzed outcomes.
criterion_notes.c5: Unit of analysis (utility/regulatory regime case), exposure (type of economic regulatory regime for water pricing), outcome (procedural consumer inclusiveness across transparency, participation, and accountability), and study design (comparative qualitative case study) are clearly identifiable.

study_design: Comparative qualitative case study (key informant interviews and legal/documentary analysis)
country: The Netherlands, Spain, and United Kingdom (Scotland)
population_and_sample: Three Western European water utility regulatory regimes (unit of analysis: regulatory regime/utility case): Vitens in The Netherlands (self-regulation), Agbar/EMA in Barcelona, Spain (bipartite negotiation), and Scottish Water/WICS in Scotland, UK (independent regulation), studied via key informant interviews and secondary/legal documents
exposure: Economic regulatory regime for water pricing and separation of policymaking from economic regulation (self-regulation vs. bipartite negotiation vs. independent regulation)
outcome: Procedural consumer inclusiveness in the water tariff-setting process, assessed qualitatively across transparency, stakeholder participation, and institutional accountability indicators
rationale: Excluded (E04: Wrong outcome). Although this is an empirical comparative case study of three water pricing regulatory regimes (Vitens in The Netherlands, Agbar in Spain, and Scottish Water/WICS in Scotland), its sole analyzed outcome is procedural consumer inclusiveness in tariff-setting governance (transparency, consultation/participation, and administrative/parliamentary accountability in Table 3). It does not examine household or community water or sanitation service access (c1=no), does not evaluate an access, connection, reliability, disconnection, or affordability outcome (c4=no; descriptive coverage and annual household water bill figures in Table 2 are background case-selection context), and under the 2026-10-13 narrow reading of Criterion 2 analyzes procedural stakeholder participation rules rather than rule-type mechanisms directly governing service access (c2=no under narrow reading, yes under plain wording; excluded under both).
